explanation: Fires on assorted tokens with no shared theme: subword pieces inside proper names (G-iff-ard, G-iff-ords, B-ok-ova, L-anzini), Latin and drug names, and function words in Romance-language text (Portuguese/Spanish/French endings and particles). There is no clear token or context that predicts strong activation.

Fires on a middle or final subword piece of a multi-token technical term, name or compound noun, once the earlier part has fixed what the word is (e.g. 'electroenceph-al-ogram', 'amy-gd-ala', 'St. Gall-en', 'insulin-like growth factor', 'right-eye image', 'reference signal'). Common in scientific and biomedical text. Ordinary words in plain prose give only weak activation.

Fires on a mixture with no common thread: code tokens such as '(!' after if/while, '#if HAVE', '.Support' and '(property', math 'sinh', and prose tokens such as 'and' in patent or biology lists and pieces of place names ('Water'bury, 'LAKE'). No single feature predicts it.

Fires on a single digit inside an identifier-like number string, usually the second or third digit after a prefix or hyphen: docket and case numbers ('NO. PD-1[2]40', '02-CR-1[3]4', '11-[4]0734'), statute and standard numbers ('ASTM F2[1]59', 'I-2[6]5'), DOI or reference IDs, and port or RFC numbers. Digits in ordinary quantities, dates or decimals give only weak activation.

Fires on a function word or modifier that comes right after a coordinating or parenthetical frame in running prose: 'and [other/its/many]', '(but [not])', 'any [other] kind', 'the previously [enumerated]', plus parts of names in legal counsel lists. Activation is broad and contextual, and no single token type dominates.

Fires on words in Christian religious or devotional text, most strongly on descriptions of God or divine action ('God is holy and [pure]', 'the Lord to [call]', 'God's [Kingdom]', 'God may have [called]'). Non-religious examples are weak, scattered and unrelated.

Fires on the first subword of a word or name in non-English text, especially Italian, French and Indian names ('Ch'awla, 'Fi'orentino, 'F'iumicino, 'p'âtes), and on the apostrophe in French elisions ('d'', 'l''). Some CJK and Finnish tokens also activate. It seems to track the onset of a foreign or romanized word after a space or apostrophe.

Fires mainly on 'agile'/'Agile' (strongest on the 'ile' piece of 'ag-ile') in the business or software-methodology sense. Related tech-process terms (DevSecOps, agility, continuous integration) activate moderately, and other tokens such as '4G' or isotope labels give a scattered weak response.

Fires on digits or short tokens inside numbers and identifiers in structured contexts: citation reference tags ('[@b[3]', '[@B[7]8]'), years, error codes and ports in code, numbers in math word problems, and module path parts in imports. It is a broad 'token inside a numeric or code identifier' response with some unrelated outliers (e.g. a Romanian word).

Fires on the token that closes a citation, sentence or reference unit just before the final punctuation: the closing ']\]' of bracketed citations, the last digit of a year before a period ('196[3].', '200[7].'), 'said' at the end of a quote attribution, and 'License' in 'limitations under the License.'. The key cue is that the next token is a period or the end of a clause.

Fires on the second part of a fixed multiword name or expression when the first part strongly predicts it ('198[4]' as Orwell's title, 'BM[J]', 'coronary artery [bypass]', 'Great Expect[ations]', '.com' after a domain, 'nothing [to]', 'out [of] bed'). It completes predictable collocations across many domains, and no single topic stands out.

Fires on 'vitro' (or 'ro' in 'in vit-ro') in the Latin phrase 'in vitro'. Similar Latin or medical prefixes and phrases ('ad hoc', 'post' in postnatal/postoperative, 'prenatal', 'in situ') give moderate to weak activation.

Fires on function words and structural tokens that follow a verb or keyword and introduce its object or argument: 'the' after a verb in scientific titles ('suppressed [the]', 'mediate [the]'), 'function' and 'TABLE' keywords in code, 'of'/'with'/'and' in license boilerplate, and colons that open an equation or error message. A general 'start of an argument' response, with no clear single concept.

Fires on internal pieces of chemical names, units and formulas ('/m' in kg/m2, locants like '4,[4]-dimethyl', 'guanine', 'polysilicon', 'sodium valproate', 'Mn(III)(9)'), as well as in some list items and names ('Guill-ermo'). Mostly chemistry and lab nomenclature, plus scattered other cases.

Fires on a mixture of mid-word subword pieces and modifiers ('irre-vers-ibly', 'intrins-ically', 'top-to-bottom', 'hand-foot'), the year digit in URLs or headers ('201[5]/'), '.org' in URLs, and assorted adjectives. There is no coherent shared feature.

Fires on the decimal point or the digits right around it in numbers that report a statistic (percentages, means, rates, e.g. '41[.]4%', '60[.]2%'). It is strongest on a digit in a DOI-like number ('215[0]7740'). Integers and digits in counts or times give weak activation.

Fires on two unrelated things: subword pieces of software/hosting product names ('Ples[k]', 'm[agento]', 'V[PS]', '$_[POST]'), and 'for' in legal counsel lines ('..., [for] defendant-appellee') along with other legal-filing words ('filed', 'contends', 'his petition'). Other prose tokens activate moderately with no pattern.

Fires on assorted tokens with no shared theme: 'from' after 'arise' or after an import, digits in patent numbers and years, words in cookie/privacy boilerplate ('personalised service', 'privacy notice'), and name pieces. No unifying feature can be seen.

Fires on the ordinal or number that labels a segment in a sequence, or the segment word itself: 'first [period]', 'Episode [1]8', 'series [4]', 'Experiment [1]', 'Division [One/Two]', 'Part [1]9', 'Chp [1]', '1st [set]', 'Act'. The context must be numbering parts, episodes, sessions or divisions.

Fires on the newline (usually '.\n') that ends a title or heading line, especially a paper or abstract title followed by body text ('...in heart failure[.\n]Patient...'). It also fires on line breaks after short headings. Sentence-ending periods inside running text give weaker activation.

Fires on file names and references in software license headers, mainly 'LICENSE' / 'license' / 'LICENSE_1_[0]' in phrases like 'see the LICENSE file' or 'accompanying file LICENSE_1_0.txt' and in licenses/LICENSE-2.0 URLs. Other file names in code ('README.md', 'test.html', 'store.php') activate moderately.
